rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cleaving and duality of verses 96–97 continue themes introduced in verse 95.
rows.anchor: The themes of “cleaving” and duality presented in v. 95 continue in these two verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first light of dawn appears to split the darkness of night, explaining God’s description as Cleaver of the dawn.
rows.anchor: the first light of dawn seems to cleave or split the darkness of night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night as repose is repeatedly presented as a mercy God grants humanity.
rows.anchor: created night for repose is invoked in several places as a mercy God has bestowed upon human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun and moon enable temporal reckoning and help determine the direction of the qiblah.
rows.anchor: as is His having created the sun and moon to be useful for reckoning time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stars provide spatial orientation when the sun and moon are absent.
rows.anchor: v. 97 mentions the stars as a means of spatial orientation by which people can be guided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The darkness can mean literal night or, symbolically, moral and intellectual error and misguidance.
rows.anchor: referring to either the physical darkness of the night or, symbolically, the moral and intellectual darkness of error and misguidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the symbolic reading, sun, moon, and stars represent distinct degrees of moral guidance and spiritual illumination.
rows.anchor: the sun, moon, and stars can represent different levels of moral guidance and spiritual illumination

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran groups these celestial bodies in Abraham’s argument and Joseph’s dream.
rows.anchor: The Quran frequently invokes the sun, moon, and stars together: for example, in Abraham’s argument in vv. 76–78 and in Joseph’s dream

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun, moon, and stars are made subject to God’s command and are described as prostrating to Him.
rows.anchor: these three kinds of celestial bodies are also described as made subservient by His Command

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses also describe the celestial bodies as prostrating to God.
rows.anchor: as prostrating to Him (22:18); see also 55:5–6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expounding the signs means explaining them in detail.
rows.anchor: that is, He explained them in detail, for a people who know

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who know possess intellect, reflect correctly, and reason from sensory experience and the seen toward the intellectual and unseen.
rows.anchor: who reason from sensory realities to intellectual ones and from the seen to the unseen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain from heaven is a sign of Divine Power and Benevolence that revives the earth.
rows.anchor: God’s sending down water from the sky is repeatedly mentioned as a sign of Divine Power and Benevolence through which He revives the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain also supplies human beings with drink.
rows.anchor: provides drink for human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water can purify people and remove Satan’s defilement.
rows.anchor: gives them a means to “purify” themselves and remove the defilement of Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran often describes water as the means by which diverse crops and fruits emerge from the earth.
rows.anchor: specifically cited as the means by which diverse crops and fruits come forth from the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shifts from third-person reference to God sending rain to first-person plural speech about bringing forth plants.
rows.anchor: The verse begins with a reference to God in the third person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distant third person evokes God’s Transcendence, while the intimate first person evokes His Immanence in every detail of earthly life.
rows.anchor: evokes God’s Transcendence relative to the earthly realm and His Immanence in all of its minute workings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variety of fruit produced by the same water invites wonder.
rows.anchor: wonder that such diverse fruits and produce come forth after being watered with the same water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse evokes God’s power to produce multiplicity from singularity, as He creates many human beings from one soul.
rows.anchor: ability to bring forth diversity and multiplicity from singularity, as when He creates the multiplicity of human beings from a single soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses cite grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates as abundant provision, sometimes in the heavenly Garden.
rows.anchor: are also found in other verses as examples of God’s bountiful provision in the world and, in some cases, in the heavenly Garden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earthly fruits and the fruits of Paradise are symbolically analogous or comparable.
rows.anchor: the fruits of the earth and of Paradise are symbolically analogous or comparable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Low-hanging date clusters suggest bounty and ease because heavy, ripe fruit is readily accessible.
rows.anchor: Clusters of dates hanging low suggests both bounty and ease, as the fruit hangs low when it is heavy and ripe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plants can resemble one another even when their produce differs greatly.
rows.anchor: the resemblance certain plants have to one another, even when their produce is very different

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resemblance and difference of produce evoke the interwoven oneness and multiplicity of creation.
rows.anchor: the interwoven nature of oneness and multiplicity in creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs in creation point to God’s Oneness, Power, and Wisdom.
rows.anchor: signs of God’s Oneness, Power, and Wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who believe are implicitly linked with those who know in verse 97 and understand in verse 98.
rows.anchor: phrase implicitly linked to a people who know in v. 97 and a people who understand in v. 98

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers alone benefit from these signs by recognizing proofs of Divine Power and Oneness; disbelievers cannot grasp them.
rows.anchor: those who believe are the real beneficiaries of these signs, for they alone are able to see in these signs the proofs of Divine Power and Oneness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The life-giving is a metaphor for spiritual awakening; the light is religious guidance, perhaps the Quran specifically.
rows.anchor: God’s giving “life” to one who was dead is a metaphor for spiritual awakening

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light by which one walks among people is a source of religious guidance, perhaps the Quran itself.
rows.anchor: a source of religious guidance, or perhaps the Quran specifically

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads the revived person as one whose soul God prepared to receive revelation’s spiritual guidance.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī interprets the one to whom God “gives life” as a reference to a person whose soul God has prepared

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī identifies the light by which one walks among people with revelation itself.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī interprets the one to whom God “gives life” as a reference to a person whose soul God has prepared to receive the spiritual guidance of revelation, and the light by which to walk among mankind as revelation itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Light commonly symbolizes spiritual guidance and revelation in this life, while the righteous also have guiding light in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Light is a common Quranic symbol for spiritual guidance and revelation, usually in this life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of walking among people by light is also used for God-given guidance in 57:28.
rows.anchor: For the idea of light as a symbol for the means by which one might walk among mankind—that is, with guidance in the world—see 57:28

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God and His messengers are elsewhere said to bring people out of darkness into light.
rows.anchor: where God or His messengers are said to bring people out of darkness into light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers readers to its discussions of light and darkness in 6:1 and 24:35.
rows.anchor: For a fuller discussion of the meaning of light and darkness (lit.“darknesses”), see 6:1c; 24:35c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison is best understood generally as one between believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: the verse is best understood as a metaphorical comparison between believers and disbelievers generally

rows.speaker: one report
rows.claim: One report connects the revelation to Ḥamzah embracing Islam after Abū Jahl insulted the Prophet: the spiritually revived Ḥamzah is unlike Abū Jahl in darkness.
rows.anchor: According to one report, after Abū Jahl insulted the Prophet, the powerful and respected Ḥamzah came to the defense of his nephew and openly embraced Islam

rows.speaker: other reports
rows.claim: Other reports identify the person given life and light as the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Other reports consider the one who is given a light by which to walk among mankind a reference to the Prophet himself

rows.speaker: reports (R, Ṭ, Ṭs)
rows.claim: Other reports identify the person given life and light as ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
rows.anchor: or to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who had initially opposed the message brought by the Prophet, but converted in Makkah

rows.speaker: reports (R, Ṭ, Ṭs)
rows.claim: Other reports identify the person given life and light as ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, an early Companion and supporter of ʿAlī.
rows.anchor: or to ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, an early Companion who later become a close supporter of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib after the Prophet’s death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly says disbelievers’ deeds are made fair-seeming; this sūrah discusses it in verses 43, 108, and 137.
rows.anchor: That the actions of the disbelievers are made to seem fair unto them is found in several places in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn are addressed directly; they had led many people astray through flowery discourse or whispering.
rows.anchor: many among mankind have you claimed refers to the many people the jinn led astray through flowery discourse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Claimed” does not mean that jinn possessed people and controlled their wills; they called or tempted people, who responded.
rows.anchor: the jinn “possessed” these human beings in the sense of controlling their will, but rather that the jinn merely called or tempted them toward wrongdoing, and that many responded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the appointed term as the onset of the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: may refer to the onset of the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the appointed term as the end of earthly lives.
rows.anchor: or simply to the end of their earthly lives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People profited from false assurances when they called on jinn for protection from harm.
rows.anchor: human beings profited from the false assurances they received by calling upon the jinn for protection against harm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn profited because people attributed to them greatness, power, and authority they did not possess.
rows.anchor: the jinn profited from this arrangement insofar as it attributed to them a greatness, power, and authority they did not actually possess

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for abode here is mathwā, whereas verse 127 uses dār.
rows.anchor: the Fire is to be their abode (here mathwā, instead of dār, as in v. 127)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God makes human wrongdoers supporters of one another in this life.
rows.anchor: may mean that God makes human wrongdoers supporters of each other in this life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God will make wrongdoers follow one another into Hellfire.
rows.anchor: that He will make them follow one another into Hellfire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that some wrongdoers are given authority over others; these senses fit the verb nuwallī.
rows.anchor: or that some wrongdoers are given authority over others (Ṭ)—all meanings within the semantic range of the verb nuwallī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After criticizing Makkan restrictions and listing four revealed prohibitions, the verse adds Jewish dietary bans as recompense for disobedience.
rows.anchor: After the criticisms of the arbitrary restrictions on eating meat observed by the Makkan idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase suggests a ban on all carnivorous beasts, a prohibition also incorporated into Islamic dietary law through Prophetic Sunnah.
rows.anchor: suggests that they are forbidden all carnivorous beasts

rows.speaker: commentators (JJ, Q, Ṭ)
rows.claim: Many Quranic commentators understand dhī ẓufur as animals with undivided toes rather than claws.
rows.anchor: to mean “with undivided toes” (JJ, Q, Ṭ)

words: شُحُومَهُمَآ إِلَّا مَا حَمَلَتْ ظُهُورُهُمَآ أَوِ ٱلْحَوَايَآ أَوْ مَا ٱخْتَلَطَ بِعَظْمٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews were forbidden ox and sheep fat except back fat, fat in the entrails, or fat mingled with other tissue.
rows.anchor: They are further forbidden the fat of oxen and sheep, except for that upon their backs or intermingled with other tissue

rows.speaker: Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī
rows.claim: These two Sunni school founders held that the fat prohibition did not apply to Muslims.
rows.anchor: Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī, held that this prohibition on fat did not pertain to Muslims

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet did not forbid a follower from eating fat during the siege of Khaybar, when he imposed other food prohibitions.
rows.anchor: the Prophet did not forbid one of his followers from eating it during the siege of Khaybar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jewish restrictions largely parallel, but do not exactly match, dietary prohibitions in Leviticus and Deuteronomy.
rows.anchor: The specific dietary prohibitions mentioned for the Jews in the present verse are largely consistent with the extensive dietary prohibitions found in Leviticus 3 and 11, as well as Deuteronomy 14, although they are not identical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leviticus 11 bans animals that walk on paws and several birds of prey, as well as animals with undivided hooves such as camels.
rows.anchor: the Israelites are forbidden “all that walk on their paws” (v. 27) and several different birds of prey, but also animals with undivided hooves, such as camels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leviticus instructs the Israelites to remove backbone and entrail fat for burning as sacrifice.
rows.anchor: the Israelites are instructed to remove the fat from the backbone and the entrails to be burned as a sacrifice

rows.speaker: Ṭb
rows.claim: One gloss explains their willful disobedience as mistreatment of needy people among themselves.
rows.anchor: their mistreatment of the needy among themselves (Ṭb)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Another gloss takes their willful disobedience simply as wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: or simply their “wrongdoing” (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran 3:93 says no divinely imposed food prohibitions applied to Israelites before the Torah was revealed.
rows.anchor: indicates that there were no Divinely imposed dietary prohibitions on the Israelites prior to the revelation of the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community comprises Israelites who neither fished on the Sabbath nor admonished those who did.
rows.anchor: those Israelites in the town who did not participate in fishing on the Sabbath, but also did not admonish those who did

rows.speaker: community
rows.claim: Those who did not admonish ask the active admonishers why they warn people God is about to destroy or severely punish.
rows.anchor: asking why they make the effort to admonish a people whom God is about to destroy or punish

rows.speaker: admonishers
rows.claim: The admonishers say they act as an excuse before God because forbidding wrong is an obligation and doing so fulfills their moral duty.
rows.anchor: they consider themselves to be obligated to “forbid wrong,” and having done so, they have fulfilled their moral duty

rows.speaker: admonishers
rows.claim: They also hope their warning will bring Sabbath violators back to reverence for God and Mosaic Law.
rows.anchor: hoped that their warnings might succeed in bringing the Sabbath violators back to reverence for God and for Mosaic Law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Sabbath violators disregarded admonitions, God saved those who forbade evil and punished the violators.
rows.anchor: God punished the violators and saved those who forbade evil—that is, by exhorting their fellow Israelites to observe the Sabbath

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators disagree about whether abstainers who did not admonish others were saved.
rows.anchor: The commentators are divided on the fate of those who abstained both from fishing on the Sabbath and from forbidding others to do so

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One reported view counts the people who abstained but did not admonish others among the saved.
rows.anchor: some consider them to be among the saved

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successors to Moses’ followers are understood as later Jews, especially religious leaders who corrupted Mosaic teaching and law by allowing commands and prohibitions to lapse.
rows.anchor: The generation who succeeded the followers of Moses is understood by commentators to refer to some later Jews, and Jewish religious leaders in particular

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators say Jewish leaders accepted bribes to ease legal requirements for certain people.
rows.anchor: Some commentators suggest that certain Jewish leaders took bribery in exchange for easing the requirements of the law for certain people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran 19:59 similarly describes Abraham’s and Israel’s descendants being succeeded by a generation that neglected prayer and followed base desires.
rows.anchor: See also 19:59, regarding the descendants of Abraham and Israel: Then they were succeeded by a generation who neglected prayer and followed base desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They take whatever fleeting worldly goods they desire, lawful or unlawful and even sinful, while assuming they will be forgiven.
rows.anchor: they take whatever they desire of fleeting, worldly things, whether they are lawful or unlawful, or even sinful, and assume they will be forgiven for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that punishment will be brief reflects overconfidence in God’s leniency attributed to some Jews.
rows.anchor: certain Jews were overly confident about God’s leniency in judgment toward them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their taking similar worldly gains again shows they are not repentant and intend to persist in disobedience.
rows.anchor: indicating that they are not truly repentant, and that their intention is to persist in their acts of disobedience

words: أَن لَّا يَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book’s covenant refers to Torah obligations, including speaking truthfully about God according to scripture.
rows.anchor: the covenantal obligations imposed on the Jews by the Torah, one of which was to speak only truthfully about God in accordance with what is taught in the scripture

words: أَن لَّا يَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scripture teaches that forgiveness belongs to those who repent and amend their ways, not those persisting in error.
rows.anchor: God’s forgiveness is only for those who are truly repentant and mend their ways, not for those who persist in their errors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses also say that the Hereafter is better for the reverent than this world.
rows.anchor: That for the reverent the Hereafter is better than this world is also mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clinging to the Book means continuing to follow the Torah’s teachings, commands, and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: Those who cling to the Book means those who continue to adhere to the teachings, commands, and prohibitions established in the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will not fail to reward the righteous for their deeds.
rows.anchor: That God does not neglect . . . the reward of those who are righteous means that He will not fail to reward them for their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews who continue to follow Torah and Mosaic law will be rewarded for good deeds, as affirmed for Jews, Sabeans, and Christians who believe and act righteously.
rows.anchor: those who are Jews and continue to follow the Torah and Mosaic Law will be rewarded for their good deeds
